section: Neem Patent Case - W.R. Grace vs India
text: What was the neem patent case? In 1994 the European Patent Office (EPO) granted patent EP0436257 to W.R. Grace & Co. and the US Department of Agriculture for a method of controlling fungal infections in plants using a hydrophobic extract of neem oil. India, joined by the Research Foundation for Science, Technology and Ecology and the International Federation of Organic Agriculture Movements, filed a legal opposition in 1995-2000 arguing the fungicidal use of neem was traditional knowledge practised and documented in India for centuries. The EPO, and later its Technical Board of Appeal, revoked the patent in 2000 and confirmed revocation in 2005 on grounds of lack of novelty and inventive step, since the claimed method was already part of Indian traditional knowledge (prior art). The case is a landmark in the global biopiracy debate and one of the principal justifications for building the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL).

What was the turmeric patent case? In 1995 the US Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) granted US Patent 5,401,504 to two researchers at the University of Mississippi Medical Center for the use of turmeric (curcumin) in wound healing. India's Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) filed a re-examination request in 1996, submitting documentary prior art including ancient Sanskrit texts and a 1953 article in the Journal of the Indian Medical Association showing turmeric's wound-healing use was long known in Ayurveda. In 1997 the USPTO revoked all six claims for lack of novelty. This was the first instance of a US patent based on the traditional knowledge of a developing country being successfully overturned, and it directly inspired the creation of TKDL.

What was the Basmati rice patent case? In 1997 the USPTO granted US Patent 5,663,484 to the Texas company RiceTec Inc. for 'Basmati rice lines and grains', covering novel rice lines and a method of selecting them. India objected that Basmati is a traditional aromatic long-grain rice grown in the Indo-Gangetic plains for centuries and that the term was being misappropriated. India's APEDA and CSIR challenged the patent in 2000. RiceTec withdrew several claims and in 2001 the USPTO struck down 15 of the 20 claims, leaving RiceTec with only three narrow hybrid lines and barring use of the generic 'Basmati' designation. The case highlighted the need to protect traditional agricultural produce through Geographical Indications, and Basmati was later registered as a GI in India.

section: Hoodia Case - San People Benefit Sharing
text: What was the Hoodia case? The Hoodia gordonii cactus of the Kalahari has been used by the San (Bushmen) people of Southern Africa for generations to suppress hunger and thirst during long hunts. In the 1990s South Africa's CSIR isolated the appetite-suppressant molecule P57, patented it and licensed it to Phytopharm and then Pfizer and later Unilever for anti-obesity products, initially without acknowledging or compensating the San. After protests and legal pressure, in 2003 a benefit-sharing agreement was signed granting the San a share of milestone payments and royalties. The Hoodia case became a leading example of Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) under the Convention on Biological Diversity and of prior-informed consent for indigenous traditional knowledge.

What was the Ayahuasca patent case? In 1986 the USPTO granted US Plant Patent 5,751 to American entrepreneur Loren Miller for a purported variety of the Banisteriopsis caapi vine ('Da Vine'), from which the sacred ceremonial brew ayahuasca is made by indigenous Amazonian peoples. The Coordinating Body of Indigenous Organizations of the Amazon Basin (COICA), with the Center for International Environmental Law, challenged the patent in 1999, arguing the plant was well known, sacred and not novel or distinctive. The USPTO initially rejected the patent in 1999 on prior-art grounds but reinstated it in 2001 on a technicality; it finally expired in 2003. The case underscored weaknesses in patent examination for indigenous plant knowledge and the importance of documented prior art.

What was the quinoa patent case? In 1994 two researchers at Colorado State University obtained US Patent 5,304,718 covering the male-sterile Apelawa variety of quinoa and hybrids derived from it, an Andean grain cultivated by indigenous Bolivian and Peruvian farmers for thousands of years. The Bolivian National Association of Quinoa Producers (ANAPQUI) and RAFI (now ETC Group) protested that the patent could threaten Andean farmers' exports and appropriated a traditional landrace without consent. Facing international opposition, the patent holders chose not to maintain the patent and it lapsed in 1998. The quinoa case is cited as an example of biopiracy of a staple food crop and of civil-society pressure defeating an inappropriate patent.

What was the Rosy Periwinkle case? The rosy periwinkle (Catharanthus roseus), native to Madagascar and used in traditional medicine, yielded the alkaloids vincristine and vinblastine, developed by Eli Lilly into highly successful chemotherapy drugs for childhood leukaemia and Hodgkin's lymphoma. The plant generated large pharmaceutical revenues, yet Madagascar and the communities holding the traditional knowledge received no share of the benefits, as the discoveries predated modern ABS frameworks. The rosy periwinkle is frequently cited as the classic case motivating the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) and the Nagoya Protocol (2010), which require prior informed consent and fair, equitable benefit sharing for use of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge.

What is the Kava case? Kava (Piper methysticum) is a Pacific Island plant whose root has been used ceremonially and medicinally across Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa and Tonga for centuries as a relaxant. From the 1990s Western companies filed numerous patents on kava extracts, standardised kavalactone preparations and anxiety/anti-stress uses, prompting Pacific nations to object that these appropriated a communally held traditional resource without consent or benefit sharing. Concerns intensified when European regulators temporarily banned kava over liver-toxicity reports, damaging island economies. The kava dispute is used as a Pacific example of biopiracy of medicinal plant knowledge and helped drive regional traditional-knowledge protection and support for the Nagoya Protocol's ABS regime.

section: Why These Cases Led to TKDL
text: Why did the neem, turmeric and basmati cases lead to the TKDL? Each early biopiracy case (turmeric 1997, neem 2000, basmati 2001) was defended by physically retrieving prior art from ancient texts written in Sanskrit, Hindi, Arabic, Persian and Urdu, translating it and submitting it to foreign patent offices - an enormously slow and costly process. India realised that patent examiners abroad could not read these languages or access classical texts, so traditional knowledge was invisible during examination. The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) was created by CSIR and the Ministry of AYUSH to convert 350,000+ formulations from 150+ classical texts into a searchable, patent-office-compatible database in five international languages, so examiners can cite it as prior art before a patent is even granted.

What was the Enola bean case? In 1999 the USPTO granted US Patent 5,894,079 to Larry Proctor for the 'Enola' yellow bean, a colour variety of the Mexican Mayocoba/Azufrado bean grown by Mexican farmers for generations. Proctor sued US importers of Mexican yellow beans, disrupting the trade. Mexico's national research institute and the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) challenged the patent, showing the bean was a known Mexican landrace lacking novelty. After a decade of re-examination and appeals, the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit upheld rejection of all claims in 2009. The Enola bean case is a leading example of misappropriation of a staple crop landrace and of the cost and delay of overturning wrongly granted patents.

What is the Maca case? Maca (Lepidium meyenii) is a high-altitude Andean root cultivated in Peru for over 2,000 years for nutrition, fertility and stamina. Around 2000-2001 US companies obtained patents on maca extracts and their use for enhancing sexual function and hormone balance. Peru objected that these patents monopolised uses long known in Andean traditional knowledge and set up a National Anti-Biopiracy Commission to monitor and challenge such filings internationally. The maca case prompted Peru to enact Law 27811 protecting collective indigenous knowledge and to press within the WTO and WIPO for mandatory disclosure of the origin of genetic resources and traditional knowledge in patent applications.

What was the Endod case? Endod (Phytolacca dodecandra), the African soapberry, has been used in Ethiopia as a traditional laundry soap and was found by Ethiopian scientist Aklilu Lemma to kill the snails that spread schistosomiasis (bilharzia). Despite this discovery based on traditional use, a US university later sought patent protection on molluscicidal uses of the plant, raising biopiracy concerns because the underlying knowledge and research originated in Ethiopia. The endod case is cited as an example of how traditional knowledge and developing-country research can be appropriated, and of the need for benefit-sharing and recognition of the original knowledge holders and investigators.

What was the Jasmine rice dispute? Thai jasmine rice (Hom Mali) is a fragrant traditional variety central to Thai agriculture and exports. In the 1990s the US company RiceTec marketed rice under the name 'Jasmati', and separately US research on developing jasmine-type rice adapted to American growing conditions alarmed Thailand, which feared loss of its export market and misuse of its traditional variety's reputation. Thailand protested through diplomatic and trade channels and moved to protect Hom Mali through geographical-indication-style measures and plant-variety laws. The jasmine rice dispute parallels the Basmati case and illustrates why exporting nations pursue GI protection for traditional named agricultural products.

What are the common lessons from the major biopiracy cases? Across the neem, turmeric, basmati, hoodia, ayahuasca, quinoa, maca and enola-bean cases, recurring lessons emerge: (1) traditional knowledge is often novelty-defeating prior art but is invisible to examiners unless documented and translated; (2) documented, dated, accessible prior art (like TKDL) is the most effective defence; (3) reactive post-grant challenges are slow and expensive, so prevention at examination is preferable; (4) genetic resources and associated knowledge need Access and Benefit Sharing under the CBD and Nagoya Protocol; (5) named traditional products (basmati, jasmine rice) are best protected through Geographical Indications; and (6) developing countries benefit from national anti-biopiracy commissions and from pressing for mandatory disclosure-of-origin rules at WIPO and the WTO.

section: How to Use Case Precedents in Opposition
text: How can the neem and turmeric precedents help me challenge a patent on traditional knowledge? The turmeric (USPTO re-examination) and neem (EPO opposition) revocations establish that documented traditional use predating the filing date is valid prior art defeating novelty and inventive step. To use these precedents in a pre-grant or post-grant opposition or a re-examination, you should: (1) identify the exact claims and the earliest priority date; (2) assemble dated documentary prior art - classical texts, TKDL entries, prior publications, or evidence of prior public use - that discloses the same subject matter before that date; (3) frame the objection under the relevant grounds (lack of novelty/inventive step, and in India also Section 3(p) of the Patents Act on traditional knowledge and Section 25 opposition grounds); and (4) cite the neem/turmeric outcomes to show patent offices have accepted traditional-knowledge prior art. TKDL access agreements let examiners verify such prior art directly.
